idiom_name: std::shared_ptr handle + detach() on mutating access (CowPtr; Qt QSharedDataPointer)
implementation_notes: The modern realization wraps the body in a std::shared_ptr and gives the handle a detach() that clones when the body is shared: if (!sp_.unique()) sp_ = std::make_shared<T>(*sp_); this is the CowPtr idiom from More C++ Idioms, with Qt's QSharedData/QSharedDataPointer as the framework version of the same idea. cppreference records that shared_ptr::unique() was deprecated in C++17 and removed in C++20 because use_count()==1 is meaningless once other threads can hold references, so treat the count as a single-threaded hint and guard a cross-thread handle with a lock or an atomic snapshot instead. The standard library itself no longer does this for you: C++11 forbids copy-on-write std::string, and container copies must copy their elements, so the detach lives in your own value type.
pitfalls: Returning references into the body (operator[], begin(), data()) hands out interior state; once such a reference escapes, the object must be treated as unshareable and deep-copied on the next copy, otherwise the holder's reference silently changes meaning (Sutter, More Exceptional C++, Items 13-16).
use_count()/unique() is not a synchronization primitive: under data races the value is meaningless, so a shared_ptr handle shared across threads needs a lock or an atomic snapshot.
Detaching on const access throws the optimization away; keep exactly one detach helper and call it only from mutating operations.

variants.name: Intrusive counted body (ATL and Qt implicit-sharing era)
variants.idiom_name: reference count embedded in the body + clone-on-write (Counted Body)
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-C++11 realization puts the count inside the body (or in a counted base class) so the handle stays one pointer and no separate control block is allocated: the handle's copy constructor increments, the destructor decrements and frees at zero, and each mutator clones when the count is greater than one. This is the shape of ATL strings and Qt's implicit sharing, and it remains the only option when the toolchain is C++98/03; on C++11 or later prefer the shared_ptr form unless the extra allocation or the ABI matters.
pitfalls: The intrusive count changes the body type and its ABI, so plain-old-data or third-party bodies cannot carry it.
Exception safety: if the body's copy constructor throws after the count was incremented, the count stays high and the body is never freed - increment after a successful clone or use a guard.
Non-atomic counts shared across threads race exactly as in the shared_ptr case; use the thread-safe copy-on-write form (atomic count) there.
